issues.explanation: Funerals/graves is hard to reconcile as a primary trigger for a life-threatening motor vehicle collision when the rest of the profile does not reference death-related loss, bereavement, or fatality cues; it stands apart from the other trigger and appraisal content in a way that is clinically difficult to explain.

Failed Role suggests a strong role-based or responsibility-based meaning of the trauma, but the rest of the profile does not indicate injury-related incapacity, inability to work, or family-protector themes that would support this appraisal. For this patient, it feels insufficiently grounded in the surrounding items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: 'Permanent humiliation' is not impossible after a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, but in this profile it sits awkwardly with the rest of the formulation and item set, which otherwise centers on fear-based post-collision threat, sensory reliving, and vulnerability rather than shame/humiliation. It is the least clinically integrated appraisal here and is hard to explain without other supporting shame-related items.

'Entrapment: Having no options' is not a clear contradiction, but for this trauma/profile it is weakly integrated compared with the other trigger items. The rest of the profile emphasizes crash reminders, reliving, danger appraisals, and hyperarousal. A strong entrapment trigger would usually be better supported by appraisals or memory content about being trapped or unable to escape, which are absent here.

vignette:
Robert, a 67-year-old European American school principal, first sought help after realizing that the driving he had once done without thought had become a source of dread, and that his nights were no longer giving him the rest he needed. The collision that changed things occurred on an ordinary afternoon while he was driving home from work. Another car came at him suddenly, the impact violent enough to leave him with the stark sense that he might not survive. In the aftermath, what stayed with him was not a clean story he could tell, but fragments that would not settle into words. He has said that he cannot seem to put the frightening event into words, even now, and when he tries to describe it, the account breaks apart into sensations and flashes. At times the memory returns like a film playing over and over, and when that happens he experiences it as if it is happening right now rather than as something safely in the past.

In the weeks and months that followed, Robert noticed that certain moments in everyday life could bring the collision back with startling force. Shouting, especially sudden raised voices, makes him tense and brace himself before he has even had time to think. Loud noises—something dropped hard in a hallway, a slam from outside, a burst of sound in a busy parking lot—can send him right back to the raw edge of that afternoon. He is also unsettled by seeing cars that have been hit by accident, because the sight seems to condense everything he fears into one image: twisted metal, helplessness, and the possibility that ordinary travel can become catastrophic in an instant. These cues are particularly powerful because they resemble the sensory chaos of the crash itself, the shock of noise, impact, and the helpless sense that danger can arrive without warning.

Robert’s understanding of himself changed after the accident as well. He has come to believe that somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, and that he has permanently changed for the worse. He speaks of the accident as though it marked him in a lasting way, leaving him less steady and less able to trust his own body and judgment. He also sees the world as a dangerous place, not in an abstract philosophical sense but as a lived expectation that danger can appear at any moment, even during ordinary routines. This sense of danger is especially pronounced when things take longer than expected. If his wife is delayed, if a meeting runs late, or if a student, staff member, or delivery is late to arrive, he quickly assumes that something bad is happening. He finds himself checking the clock, trying to make sense of the delay, and feeling his body tighten as if something ominous must be unfolding just beyond his view.

At work, these reactions have made daily life harder. As principal, Robert still goes to the school, but doing so has become an effort. He has begun avoiding going to work on some days, especially when he feels poorly rested or already on edge, and he pushes himself only because he knows his responsibilities will not disappear. The school environment itself can be difficult: loud hallway noise, sudden shouting from students, and unexpected interruptions can all catch him off guard. He remains outwardly composed much of the time, but he is privately working hard to keep himself together. He has tried to force himself to think only positive thoughts, telling himself to stay calm and not dwell on what happened, but this effort leaves him feeling no more settled. Instead, he often feels unable to relax even when he knows he is in a safe place, sitting in his own home or in his office with the doors closed.

At night, the strain becomes harder to manage. Robert has trouble falling asleep and also wakes during the night, alert for sounds and thoughts he does not want. When he cannot settle, he eats excessively to manage the distress, telling himself that at least the food gives him something immediate and concrete to do. It offers brief relief, though not the kind that restores his sense of calm. His wife has noticed that he seems less easygoing and more preoccupied, and Robert himself is aware that the changes have narrowed his life. He has not come for help because he believes the danger is gone; rather, he has come because the fear has continued to follow him into work, home, and sleep, and he is frightened by how frequently the past now arrives in the present. What he most wants is to sleep through the night, to drive and work without bracing for disaster, and to feel again that an ordinary day can stay ordinary.
